main.claim: Upload a photo of your handwritten notes and get the text back in a few seconds. The AI types it out line by line, keeps the line breaks and marks any word it cannot read as [?]. Free, with no account needed.

sections.heading: How to turn handwriting into text
sections.body:
Take a clear photo of the page, or save a picture of it. Then open the tool and choose the image when the page asks for a file. Image files up to 15 MB work, so a normal phone photo fits.

1. Photograph the page in good light, lying flat, with all the writing in frame.
2. Open [Handwriting to Text](https://handwriting-to-text.lazur.app/).
3. Choose your photo. The file must be an image, such as a JPG or PNG.
4. Wait a few seconds. The text appears on the page.
5. Select copy to put the whole text on your clipboard.

Read the result once against the page. The reader is a computer, so it can confuse letters that look alike, such as a 1 and an l, or a u and a v. Fix those by hand before you use the text.

sections.heading: What you get back
sections.body:
The tool types out the text as it reads it and keeps the line breaks from your page. You get the text only. The tool adds no comments, summary or title.

Where a word is unreadable, you see **[?]** in its place. That mark shows you exactly where to look, so you do not have to compare every line with the page. Check each [?] against the photo, type in the right word, and then read the rest once for anything that looks wrong.

A page usually comes back in about 1 to 3 seconds. The tool works on image files only, so if your notes are in a PDF, save each page as an image first and run the pages one at a time.

sections.heading: Photos that give the cleanest text
sections.body:
A flat, well lit page gives the reader the clearest lines. Hold the phone above the page and keep it parallel to the paper, so the lines do not slope. Avoid shadows from your hand, a lamp or the phone itself across the writing.

Keep the whole page in one photo. Half a line at the edge is harder to read than a full line in the middle of the frame. Dark ink on light paper gives the best contrast. Pencil on a grey or lined page can be faint, so a photo with the light from the side often shows it better.

If a result has many [?] marks, take the photo again with more light and a straighter angle, then run it once more.

sections.heading: Your photo and your privacy
sections.body:
The tool sends your photo to Lazur's servers, where Google Gemini reads the handwriting and returns the text. Do not upload a page with bank details, passwords or other private information that you would not want that service to read.

You do not need an account. You get 3 free runs a day. After those, you get 3 more when you leave an email address.

Lazur is a Mac app: hold two keys and talk, and it types into whatever app you are in. If you dictate every day, Lazur does that in any app on your Mac.

pages.title: Handwriting to Text on iPad: Free Photo Converter | Lazur
pages.description: Turn handwriting on your iPad into typed text. Scribble converts your pencil writing live, and this free tool reads a photo of paper notes in seconds.
pages.claim: On an iPad, Apple Pencil's Scribble turns your handwriting into text as you write in a text field. To convert notes you already wrote on paper, take a photo, choose it in this free tool, and copy the text it returns.

sections.heading: Write with Scribble and Apple Pencil
sections.body:
Scribble is built into iPadOS. Write with Apple Pencil in any text field, and Scribble converts your handwriting to typed text. It still works when your writing runs past the edge of the field. Apple says Scribble runs directly on the iPad, so your writing stays on the device.

Scribble needs an Apple Pencil, which is sold separately, and a supported iPad. Its toolbar actions depend on the app you are using. In Notes and Freeform, open the tool palette and tap the Handwriting tool, which sits to the left of the pen, then write.

You can edit with the pencil too. Scratch out a word to delete it, touch and hold to insert text, and draw a vertical line to join or split characters.

sections.heading: Turn Scribble on or off
sections.body:
Scribble is set in Settings. Open Settings, tap Apple Pencil, and turn Scribble on or off. Apple's support guide gives this path for turning Scribble off, and the same screen controls it.

If you do not write with the pencil, you can leave Scribble off. It does not change how the photo tool works.

sections.heading: Convert a photo of paper notes on iPad
sections.body:
Scribble only converts while you write with the pencil. If your notes are on paper, or you wrote them before you had the iPad, use a photo instead.

1. Take a photo of the page in good light, or save a picture of it to Photos.
2. Open [Handwriting to Text](https://handwriting-to-text.lazur.app/) in your iPad browser.
3. Choose the photo when the page asks for a file. Images up to 15 MB work.
4. Wait a few seconds for the text to appear.
5. Select copy, then paste the text into Notes, Pages or any other app.

The tool marks words it cannot read as [?]. Look at each one against the photo, type the right word in, and read the rest once.

sections.heading: Scribble or the photo tool
sections.body:
Use Scribble when you want text in a text field right now, as you write with the pencil. Use the photo tool when the handwriting already exists on paper or in a picture, and you want an editable copy.

The photo tool does not see your pencil strokes. It reads one finished image of a page and returns a block of text. It is free, and each day you get 3 runs. Leave an email address and you get 3 more.

Pick the method before you start. If you are writing a new note, open the note app and write with the pencil. If you are copying an old note, take the photo, run it through the tool and copy the text in one go, so you do not lose the page while you switch between apps. Keep the photo until you have checked the text.

faq.q: How do I activate handwriting on iPad?
faq.a: Open Settings, tap Apple Pencil, and check that Scribble is turned on. You need an Apple Pencil and a supported iPad. In Notes, open the tool palette and tap the Handwriting tool, then write with the pencil.

faq.q: Is there an iPad app that converts handwriting to text?
faq.a: Scribble is built into iPadOS, so you do not need to install an app for it. For a photo of paper notes, this free tool runs in your iPad browser with nothing to install. You get 3 free runs a day, and 3 more after you leave an email address.

faq.q: How do I convert my handwriting to typed text?
faq.a: On an iPad with Apple Pencil, write in any text field and Scribble converts the writing as you go. For notes on paper, take a clear photo, choose it in the free tool and copy the text. Check each [?] mark against the photo before you use the text.

pages.h1: Handwriting to text with Apple Pencil
pages.claim: Apple Pencil converts handwriting live with Scribble, in any text field on iPad. For notes you already wrote, this free tool reads a photo of the page and returns the text, with [?] marking words it cannot read.

sections.heading: What Scribble does with Apple Pencil
sections.body:
Scribble is Apple's feature for writing with Apple Pencil. Write in a text field, and Scribble converts your handwriting to typed text as you write. It works even when your writing extends past the edge of the field.

You can edit with the pencil as well. Scratch out a word to delete it, touch and hold to insert text, draw a vertical line to join or separate characters, and circle or underline text to select it.

Scribble needs an Apple Pencil, sold separately, and a supported iPad. Apple says it is available in several languages. Check Apple's feature availability page for your language before you rely on it.

sections.heading: Where to find Scribble
sections.body:
Scribble is controlled in Settings. Open Settings, tap Apple Pencil, and turn Scribble on or off there. In Notes and Freeform, open the tool palette and tap the Handwriting tool, which sits to the left of the pen.

If you do not use the pencil to write, turn Scribble off and the rest of iPadOS works as before.

sections.heading: Convert a photo when the notes are on paper
sections.body:
Apple Pencil only converts the writing you make with it. Handwriting from a notebook, a whiteboard or a class handout needs a photo.

1. Take a photo of the page in good light, with the whole text in frame.
2. Open [Handwriting to Text](https://handwriting-to-text.lazur.app/) in your browser.
3. Choose the photo. Image files up to 15 MB work.
4. Wait a few seconds, then select copy.

Check every [?] mark against the photo and type the right word. Read the rest once, because a reader can confuse letters that look alike, such as a 1 and an l.

Hold the iPad or phone still while you take the photo, and make sure no line is cut off at the edges of the frame. Once the text appears, read it while the page is still in front of you. It is quicker to fix one [?] now than to hunt for that line later.

sections.heading: Pick the right tool for the job
sections.body:
Scribble converts while you write, so the text lands in the field you are using. The photo tool does not see your strokes. It reads a finished image and gives you a block of text to edit.

Use Scribble to write new text with the pencil. Use the photo tool to turn notes you already have into text you can edit. Each day you get 3 free runs, and 3 more after you leave an email address.

The two methods do not conflict. You can write new notes with Scribble and keep photos of the paper pages you still need. Pick the method that matches each page, and you will not have to choose one for all of your notes.

faq.q: Can I convert my handwriting to text using my iPad pencil?
faq.a: Yes, with Scribble. Write with Apple Pencil in any text field, and Scribble converts your handwriting to typed text. You need an Apple Pencil and a supported iPad, and Apple says Scribble runs directly on the iPad.

faq.q: Can you convert handwriting to text on an iPad?
faq.a: Yes. With an Apple Pencil, Scribble does it live as you write. Without a pencil, take a photo of your handwritten notes and use the free tool here. It returns the text and marks words it cannot read with [?].

faq.q: How do I convert my handwriting to typed text?
faq.a: For writing you do now, use Scribble with Apple Pencil in a text field. For notes on paper, take a clear photo, choose it in the free tool, and copy the text. Check each [?] mark against the photo before you use the text.

pages.title: Best Handwriting to Text App: Which One to Use | Lazur
pages.description: Find the right handwriting to text app for your notes. Compare live pen tools with photo converters, and see when a free browser tool fits.
pages.claim: No single app suits every case, because the right tool depends on where your handwriting is. Use a live tool such as Scribble or OneNote's Ink to Text pen while you write, and a photo tool like this free one for notes already on paper.

sections.heading: Choose by where your handwriting is
sections.body:
Handwriting to text tools fall into two groups. Live tools turn your writing into text as you write with a pen or stylus. Photo tools read a picture of a page you already wrote.

If you write on a tablet or a computer with a pen, start with what your device already offers. On an iPad, that is Scribble, which works with Apple Pencil in any text field. On Windows 11, OneNote has an Ink to Text pen for digital pens. If your notes are on paper, you need a photo tool, and that is where this free tool fits.

A quick test helps. Ask where the ink lives. If the writing is on the screen as you make it, a live tool fits. If the writing is on the page, a photo tool fits.

sections.heading: Built-in options on your device
sections.body:
Scribble on iPad needs an Apple Pencil and a supported iPad. You turn it on or off in Settings, then Apple Pencil.

The Ink to Text pen in OneNote needs Windows 11 version 23H2 with the KB5031455 update, and it works only with a digital pen or stylus. Microsoft lists these languages: English, Spanish, Japanese, French, German, Portuguese (Brazil), Italian, Simplified Chinese and Korean. The language follows your Windows input language, so check that before you rely on it.

sections.heading: Apps on phones and other tools
sections.body:
Many handwriting apps for phones and tablets offer recognition, but they differ in what they read. Some read live writing, some read photos, and some read both. Some have a free trial or limited free use, and prices vary by region.

Before you install an app, check the store page for the current price, the inputs it supports and the languages it reads. Choose by the input you have, not by a list that ranks apps in a fixed order.

sections.heading: When this free tool is the right choice
sections.body:
Use this tool when you have a photo of handwritten notes and need the text. It runs in your browser, so there is nothing to install. Each run reads one image up to 15 MB, and it returns text with line breaks and [?] marks for words it cannot read.

You get 3 free runs a day, and 3 more after you leave an email address. Check the text against the photo before you use it.

There is no login, so copy the text into the app where you keep your notes before you close the page. Each photo is a separate run, which means a multi-page set takes one run per page.

Lazur is a Mac app that types what you say in any app. If you dictate every day, Lazur does that in any app on your Mac.

faq.q: What is the best way to convert handwriting to text?
faq.a: Match the method to your notes. Write with a digital pen in a notes app that converts live, or take a clear photo of a page you already wrote and run it through the free tool here. Read the result once and fix any [?] marks.

faq.q: Can my iPhone turn handwriting into text?
faq.a: Apple describes Scribble on its support pages for iPad with Apple Pencil. For a photo of handwritten notes on an iPhone, open the free tool in your browser, choose the photo from your library, and copy the text it returns.

faq.q: Do I need to install an app to convert handwriting?
faq.a: No, not for the photo tool. It runs in your browser, so you open the page, choose an image and copy the text. Scribble on iPad and the Ink to Text pen in OneNote are built into their platforms, so they need no separate app.

pages.title: Handwriting to Text for Windows: Pen and Photo Options | Lazur
pages.description: Convert handwriting to text on Windows with OneNote's Ink to Text pen, or turn a photo of paper notes into text in your browser for free.
pages.claim: On Windows 11, OneNote's Ink to Text pen converts handwriting as you write with a digital pen. For a photo of paper notes on any Windows PC, open this free tool in your browser, choose the picture and copy the text.

sections.heading: Use the Ink to Text pen in OneNote
sections.body:
OneNote's Ink to Text pen turns your handwriting into text as you write. Only a digital pen or stylus works. Microsoft lists these requirements:

- Windows 11 version 23H2 with the KB5031455 update installed
- OneNote for Microsoft 365
- A Windows input language from this list: English, Spanish, Japanese, French, German, Portuguese (Brazil), Italian, Simplified Chinese or Korean

You edit with pen gestures. Draw up-and-down squiggles over words to delete them, and draw a straight line through text to select it. Write over a selection to replace it, and draw a backwards L at the end of a sentence to start a new line. Microsoft lists the same gestures for Word and PowerPoint.

sections.heading: Convert a photo of paper notes
sections.body:
The pen only works on writing you make with it. Notes from a notebook or a class handout need a photo.

1. Photograph the page in good light, or scan it and save the image file.
2. Open [Handwriting to Text](https://handwriting-to-text.lazur.app/) in your browser on Windows.
3. Choose the image file. Files up to 15 MB work.
4. Wait a few seconds for the text, then select copy.

Paste the text into Word, Notepad or any other app. Check each [?] mark against the image and type in the right word.

Frame the photo so the page is upright and the lines run left to right. A sideways page is harder to read and can leave more [?] marks. Turn the phone or the scan so the text is straight, then choose the file. Because there is no login, copy the text somewhere safe before you close the browser tab.

sections.heading: Why the pen and the photo tool differ
sections.body:
The pen converts while you write, inside OneNote, so the text lands on the page you are working on. The photo tool works on a finished image. It returns plain text with line breaks, and it does not read live pen strokes.

Use the pen when you are writing new notes on a supported Windows 11 device. Use the photo tool when the handwriting is already on paper or in a file. Each day you get 3 free runs, and 3 more after you leave an email address.

sections.heading: Lazur on Windows
sections.body:
Lazur is a Mac app for now, and a Windows version is coming. Until then, the free handwriting tool above works in your browser on Windows. It needs no install and no account, so you can use it on a work PC where you cannot add software.

If you dictate on your Mac every day, Lazur types what you say into any app. On Windows, use the OneNote pen for live writing and this tool for photos.

faq.q: How can I convert my handwriting to computer text?
faq.a: On Windows 11, use the Ink to Text pen in OneNote with a digital pen or stylus, and the text appears as you write. For notes on paper, take a photo or scan the page, run it through the free tool, and copy the output. Check each [?] mark.

faq.q: What do I need to use the Ink to Text pen?
faq.a: You need Windows 11 version 23H2 with the KB5031455 update, OneNote for Microsoft 365, and a digital pen or stylus. Microsoft says the language follows your Windows input language, and lists nine supported languages on its help page.

faq.q: How do I convert a photo of handwriting to text?
faq.a: Open the free tool in your browser, choose the image file, and wait a few seconds. The text appears with line breaks kept. Words the tool cannot read show as [?], so check those against the photo before you paste the text anywhere.
